_doc: Naming data for generated people. Pick cultures active at the year (start<=year<=end) whose region box [lon_min, lat_min, lon_max, lat_max] contains the place; prefer the smallest box. Cultures with minority=true are for characters of that community only. Pattern placeholders: {given}, {family}, {father} (a random male given name of the same culture), {place} (home place name), {byname} (a random entry of bynames, which may itself contain placeholders). pattern_female overrides pattern for women when present.

cultures.name: Sumerian / Old Akkadian / Old Babylonian
cultures.note: Single theophoric names (Sumerian 'Ur-X' servant of god X, 'Lu-X' man of X; Akkadian sentence names like Sin-iddinam 'Sin has given'). Identity was given by filiation and office. Includes Old Assyrian merchants of Kanesh (Pushu-ken, Imdi-ilum).

sources.cite: Cuneiform Digital Library Initiative (CDLI)
Larsen, M. T., Ancient Kanesh: A Merchant Colony in Bronze Age Anatolia (2015)

cultures.name: Middle/Neo-Assyrian & Babylonian (Akkadian)
cultures.note: Akkadian sentence names ('Nabu has protected the brother'); in 1st-millennium Babylonia, urban families added an ancestor name (Egibi, Nur-Sin) as a family line: 'X son of Y descendant of Z'. Cuneiform naming persisted in Hellenistic Uruk (Anu-uballit).

sources.cite: The Prosopography of the Neo-Assyrian Empire (PNA), Oracc
Wunsch, C., Das Egibi-Archiv (2000); Oracc Babylonian archives

cultures.name: Old & Middle Kingdom Egyptian
cultures.note: Single personal names, often theophoric or invoking the king; filiation 'born of' the mother was common in the Middle Kingdom. Titles defined social identity.

sources.cite: Ranke, H., Die ägyptischen Personennamen (1935-77)
Digital Egypt for Universities, UCL

cultures.name: New Kingdom & Late Period Egyptian
cultures.note: Single names; non-elite workers at Deir el-Medina (Paneb, Naunakhte) are well documented. Late Period names often 'Padi-X' (the one whom god X gave).

sources.cite: Černý, J., A Community of Workmen at Thebes in the Ramesside Period (1973)
Deir el-Medina Database, Leiden University

cultures.name: Hittite & Luwian Anatolian
cultures.note: Single names of Hattic, Hittite, Luwian (-ziti 'man', -muwa 'might') or Hurrian (-hepa, -teshub) origin. Female names thinly attested outside royalty; list is short.

sources.cite: Laroche, E., Les noms des Hittites (1966)
Hethitologie Portal Mainz

cultures.name: Phoenician & Punic
cultures.note: Theophoric names on Baal, Melqart, Eshmun, Ashtart, Tanit (Abd- 'servant of', Bod- 'by the hand of'); Punic inscriptions give long genealogies 'X son of Y son of Z'. Greek/Latin forms (Hannibal, Hamilcar) are used here alongside Semitic ones.

sources.cite: Benz, F. L., Personal Names in the Phoenician and Punic Inscriptions (1972)
Jongeling, K., Handbook of Neo-Punic Inscriptions (2008)

cultures.name: Ancient Israelite & Second Temple Jewish
cultures.note: Yahwistic names (-yahu, Yeho-) dominate Iron Age seals and ostraca (Lachish, Arad); Second Temple ossuaries show a narrow pool (Shimon, Yosef, Yehudah, Miryam, Shelamzion) plus Greek names.

sources.cite: Ilan, T., Lexicon of Jewish Names in Late Antiquity, Part I (2002)
Avigad, N. & Sass, B., Corpus of West Semitic Stamp Seals (1997)

cultures.name: Archaic & Classical Greek
cultures.note: One personal name plus patronymic (genitive) and, for citizens abroad, an ethnic ('of Miletos'); at Athens the deme name was added. Names are compounds (Kallikrates 'fine power') or short forms.

sources.cite: Lexicon of Greek Personal Names (LGPN), Oxford
Hornblower, S. & Matthews, E. (eds.), Greek Personal Names: Their Value as Evidence (2000)

cultures.name: Hellenistic & Roman-era Greek East
cultures.note: Greek names spread across the Macedonian kingdoms; in Egypt papyri show Greek/Egyptian double names. Under Rome, citizens took Aurelios/Flavios as a prefix (Aurelios Isidoros). Bactria box covers Greco-Bactrian settlers.

sources.cite: Trismegistos People database
Lexicon of Greek Personal Names (LGPN)

cultures.name: Roman (Latin)
cultures.note: Men: praenomen + nomen (gens) + cognomen; by the Empire most were known by nomen + cognomen, here '{family} {given}' (add a praenomen from the last entries for formality). Women used the feminine nomen plus a cognomen (list holds full names). Freedmen took their patron's nomen.

sources.cite: Kajanto, I., The Latin Cognomina (1965)
Vindolanda Tablets Online
Epigraphik-Datenbank Clauss-Slaby

cultures.name: Gaulish & Ancient British Celtic
cultures.note: Compound names (-rix 'king', -maros 'great', -genos 'born of'); mostly known from coins, Caesar, and Gallo-Latin inscriptions. Female names from inscriptions, often Latinized.

sources.cite: Evans, D. Ellis, Gaulish Personal Names (1967)
Delamarre, X., Noms de personnes celtiques (2007)

cultures.name: Byzantine Greek
cultures.note: Christian given names; hereditary family names appear among the aristocracy from the 9th-10th c. and spread widely by the Palaiologan era. Before ~900 use given name plus byname or place.

sources.cite: Prosopography of the Byzantine World (PBW)
Prosopographisches Lexikon der Palaiologenzeit (PLP)

cultures.name: Achaemenid Persian (Old Persian)
cultures.note: Iranian compound names (Mithra-data 'given by Mithra', -farnah 'glory'), known from Old Persian, Elamite Persepolis tablets (Parnakka, Irdabama) and Greek renderings. Female names are sparse.

sources.cite: Tavernier, J., Iranica in the Achaemenid Period (ca. 550-330 B.C.) (2007)
Persepolis Fortification Archive Project, Univ. of Chicago

cultures.name: Parthian & Sasanian Iranian (Middle Persian)
cultures.note: Middle Persian names with Zoroastrian theophoric elements (Adur- 'fire', Mihr-, -dukht 'daughter'); great houses (Suren, Karin, Mihran) used as clan names.

sources.cite: Gignoux, P., Noms propres sassanides en moyen-perse épigraphique (Iranisches Personennamenbuch II/2, 1986)
Encyclopaedia Iranica

cultures.name: New Persian (Islamic Iran, Samanid to Qajar)
cultures.note: Arabic-Islamic and Shahnama-epic given names; identity via nisba (place of origin), laqab and kunya. Surnames were legally required only from 1925; for 1900s add a family name from the bynames.

sources.cite: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Names, Personal'
Schimmel, A., Islamic Names (1989)

cultures.name: Sogdian (Silk Road Iranian)
cultures.note: Theophoric names on the goddess Nanai and on farn 'glory'; Sogdian traders in China took Chinese surnames by origin city (An = Bukhara, Kang = Samarkand, Shi = Kesh). Female list thin (Ancient Letters, Mount Mugh).

sources.cite: Lurje, P., Personal Names in Sogdian Texts (Iranisches Personennamenbuch II/8, 2010)
de la Vaissière, É., Sogdian Traders: A History (2005)

cultures.name: Pre-Islamic & Early Islamic Arabic
cultures.note: Ism + nasab ('son of'), with kunya (Abu X 'father of X') and tribal nisba (al-Qurashi, al-Tamimi). Pre-Islamic 'Abd + deity' names gave way to Abd + divine attribute.

sources.cite: Caskel, W., Gamharat an-nasab: Das genealogische Werk des Hisam ibn Muhammad al-Kalbi (1966)
Onomasticon Arabicum, IRHT-CNRS

cultures.name: Medieval Arabic (Abbasid to Mamluk Middle East)
cultures.note: Full form is kunya + ism + nasab + laqab + nisba (e.g. Abu al-Qasim Ahmad ibn Yusuf al-Baghdadi). Honorific '-al-Din' laqabs become personal names after the 11th c.; Mamluks bore Turkic names.

sources.cite: Onomasticon Arabicum, IRHT-CNRS
Schimmel, A., Islamic Names (1989)
Goitein, S. D., A Mediterranean Society (1967-93) [Geniza traders]

cultures.name: Maghrebi & Andalusi Arabic / Amazigh
cultures.note: Arabic naming as in the East, with Maghrebi preference for kunya 'Abu' and Iberian forms (Lubb, Fortun among muwallads). Amazigh names (Ziri, Buluggin, Tashfin, Tinhinan, Itto) common in the Maghreb.

sources.cite: Marín, M. et al., Prosopografía de los ulemas de al-Andalus (PUA)
Onomasticon Arabicum, IRHT-CNRS

cultures.name: Modern Arabic
cultures.note: Given name + father's name + grandfather's or family name; fixed surnames became standard in the 20th c. (Ottoman/Egyptian civil registers). Christian Arabs use biblical/Western names.

sources.cite: Schimmel, A., Islamic Names (1989)
Wikipedia, 'Arabic name'

cultures.name: Ottoman Turkish
cultures.note: Given name plus descriptive or patronymic byname (oğlu 'son of'), place, or title (Ağa, Efendi, Paşa, Bey, Hanım). Surnames mandatory only from 1934.

sources.cite: Ottoman Turkish onomastics: Türk Dil Kurumu, Kişi Adları Sözlüğü
Wikipedia, 'Turkish name'

cultures.name: Modern Turkish (Republic)
cultures.note: Surname Law of 1934 gave every family a Turkish surname, often descriptive (Yılmaz 'undaunted', Demir 'iron') or occupational.

sources.cite: Türk Dil Kurumu, Kişi Adları Sözlüğü
TÜİK (Turkish Statistical Institute) name statistics

cultures.name: Medieval Sephardic & Mizrahi Jewish
cultures.note: Hebrew names alongside Arabic or Romance vernacular forms (Vidal = Hayyim, Bonafos). Iberian families had stable surnames (Ibn Ezra, Abravanel). minority: the simulation should choose this list only for Jewish characters, not as the majority culture of a region.

sources.cite: Goitein, S. D., A Mediterranean Society (1967-93)
Laredo, A. I., Las nombres en la Cultura Sefardí; and Avotaynu name studies

cultures.name: Ashkenazi Jewish
cultures.note: Hebrew sacred names paired with Yiddish kinnuim (Zvi-Hirsch, Aryeh-Leib, Dov-Ber). Hereditary surnames imposed in Austria (1787), Prussia (1812) and Russia (1804); before that, patronymic '{given} ben {father}' or house/town names. minority: use for Jewish characters only.

sources.cite: Beider, A., A Dictionary of Ashkenazic Given Names (2001)
Beider, A., A Dictionary of Jewish Surnames from the Russian Empire (2008)

cultures.name: Armenian
cultures.note: Single names with patronymics in early periods; noble houses (nakharar: Mamikonian, Bagratuni) as clan names. Modern surnames in -ian/-yan 'son of' derived from a forebear's name or trade (19th c. standard).

sources.cite: Acharian, H., Dictionary of Armenian Personal Names (Hayots andznanunneri bararan, 1942-62)
Wikipedia, 'Armenian name'

cultures.name: Georgian
cultures.note: Christian and native given names; noble houses (Orbeliani, Dadiani, Chavchavadze) and later universal surnames in -shvili 'child of', -dze 'son of', -ia/-ua (Mingrelian), -ani (Svan).

sources.cite: Georgian onomastic dictionary, National Parliamentary Library of Georgia
Wikipedia, 'Georgian name'

cultures.name: Roman & Coptic Egyptian
cultures.note: Greek, Egyptian and biblical names side by side in papyri and Coptic letters; Apa 'father' marks monks; T(a)- prefix 'she of' in female names.

sources.cite: Trismegistos People database
Hasitzka, M., Namen in koptischen dokumentarischen Texten (2007)

cultures.name: Ethiopian (Ge'ez / Amharic / Tigrinya)
cultures.note: No surnames: a person is known by given name followed by father's given name. Christian theophoric compounds (Gebre 'servant of', Wolde 'son of', Walatta 'daughter of', Hayle 'power of').

sources.cite: Encyclopaedia Aethiopica (Uhlig, ed., 2003-14)
Wikipedia, 'Ethiopian name'

cultures.name: Christian Nubian (Old Nubian)
cultures.note: Greek/biblical Christian names together with Old Nubian names, often with -kouda 'servant' (Mariankouda 'servant of Mary'); attested in documents from Qasr Ibrim and Faras. Lists are short by necessity.

sources.cite: Ochała, G., Database of Medieval Nubian Texts (DBMNT)
Ruffini, G., Medieval Nubia: A Social and Economic History (2012)

cultures.name: Mande (Mali & Songhai empires, Sahel)
cultures.note: Clan names (jamu) such as Keita, Traoré, Konaté are ancient and tied to roles (Kouyaté griots, Fofana scholars). Islamic given names mixed with Mande ones.

sources.cite: Conrad, D. C., Sunjata: A New Prose Version (2016) and Mande studies
Levtzion, N. & Hopkins, J. F. P., Corpus of Early Arabic Sources for West African History (1981)

cultures.name: Hausa
cultures.note: Islamic and Hausa day/circumstance names (Laraba 'Wednesday', Tanko 'boy after girls', Ladi 'Sunday'); people known by name + father's name, plus office titles (Sarki, Galadima, Madawaki).

sources.cite: Smith, M. G., Government in Kano 1350-1950 (1997)
Palmer, H. R., The Kano Chronicle (1908)

cultures.name: Yoruba
cultures.note: Names chosen for circumstance of birth (Taiwo/Kehinde twins, Idowu child after twins), family lineage (Ade- 'crown', Ogun-, Ifa-, Oya- for orisa devotion), and oriki praise names. Fixed surnames from the 19th-20th c.

sources.cite: Akinnaso, F. N., 'The Sociolinguistic Basis of Yoruba Personal Names', Anthropological Linguistics 22 (1980)
Johnson, S., The History of the Yorubas (1921)

cultures.name: Akan (Asante, Fante)
cultures.note: Every person bears a kradin (soul name) from the weekday of birth (Kwasi/Akosua Sunday ... Kwame/Ama Saturday) plus a name from the father's line or circumstances.

sources.cite: Agyekum, K., 'The Sociolinguistic of Akan Personal Names', Nordic Journal of African Studies 15 (2006)
Wilks, I., Asante in the Nineteenth Century (1975)

cultures.name: Swahili Coast
cultures.note: Islamic Arabic names with Bantu forms (Daudi, Athumani) and kinship prefixes (Mwana- 'child of', Mwinyi 'lord'); patrician lineages (Mazrui, Nabhani) and 'bin/binti' patronymics.

sources.cite: Pouwels, R., Horn and Crescent: Cultural Change and Traditional Islam on the East African Coast (1987)
Kilwa Chronicle (Freeman-Grenville, The Medieval History of the Coast of Tanganyika, 1962)

cultures.name: Kongo (Kingdom of Kongo)
cultures.note: Kongo names often reference birth circumstances (Nsimba/Nzuzi for twins) and lineage (kanda); after 1491 elites took Portuguese Christian names joined to Kongo names (Afonso Mvemba a Nzinga). 'a' = 'of' in genealogical names.

sources.cite: Thornton, J., The Kongolese Saint Anthony (1998); A History of West Central Africa to 1850 (2020)
Hilton, A., The Kingdom of Kongo (1985)

cultures.name: Nguni (Zulu, Xhosa, Swazi, Ndebele)
cultures.note: Meaningful names given by elders (Themba 'hope'); clan names (isibongo) such as Zulu, Ntuli, Dlamini are inherited and recited with praise names.

sources.cite: Koopman, A., Zulu Names (2002)
Bryant, A. T., Olden Times in Zululand and Natal (1929)

cultures.name: Classical India (Sanskrit / Prakrit)
cultures.note: Single names, often theophoric (-datta 'given by', -deva, -gupta 'protected', -sena 'army'); identified by father, gotra, varna/jati and town. Buddhist donative inscriptions (Sanchi, Bharhut) give many ordinary names.

sources.cite: Mehendale, M. A., Historical Grammar of Inscriptional Prakrits; Lüders, H., A List of Brahmi Inscriptions (1912)
Malalasekera, G. P., Dictionary of Pali Proper Names (1937)

cultures.name: Tamil (Sangam to Nayaka)
cultures.note: Tamil names prefixed by the father's initial or name and village; Sangam poets known by epithets. Chola inscriptions record donors with village and title (Udaiyan, Kizhan).

sources.cite: Karashima, N., A Concordance of the Names in the Cola Inscriptions (1978)
Zvelebil, K., Tamil Literature (1974)

cultures.name: Medieval & Mughal North India (Hindi/Persianate)
cultures.note: Hindus: given name + caste/clan name (Singh, Das, Rai) or title; Muslims: Persian-Arabic names with titles (Khan, Mirza, Mir, Shaikh) granted by the court. Merchants (Jain/Vania) named by firm.

sources.cite: Ali, M. Athar, The Apparatus of Empire: Awards of Ranks, Offices and Titles to the Mughal Nobility (1985)
Banarasidas, Ardhakathanak (1641), trans. Chowdhury (2009)

cultures.name: Bengali
cultures.note: Given name + caste-associated surname (Brahmin: Banerjee/Bandyopadhyay, Mukherjee, Chatterjee; Kayastha: Bose, Ghosh, Mitra, Dutta); Muslim names with Sayyid, Khan, Chowdhury.

sources.cite: Inden, R., Marriage and Rank in Bengali Culture (1976)
Banglapedia, National Encyclopedia of Bangladesh

cultures.name: Sinhala (Sri Lanka)
cultures.note: Ancient single names (Tissa, Abhaya, Naga) in Brahmi cave inscriptions; later ge names (house names) precede the given name, and under colonial rule Portuguese surnames (Perera, de Silva) spread.

sources.cite: Paranavitana, S., Inscriptions of Ceylon Vol. I (1970)
Geiger, W., The Mahavamsa (1912)

cultures.name: Chinese (Zhou / Spring & Autumn / Warring States)
cultures.note: Aristocratic men had a clan name (xing), lineage name (shi), personal name (ming) and courtesy name (zi); women were known by birth order plus clan name (Bo Ji, Meng Jiang). Lineage shi became general surnames under Qin-Han.

sources.cite: China Biographical Database (CBDB), Harvard
Wilkinson, E., Chinese History: A New Manual (2018), ch. on names
Yuan, Haiwang, & Shi Ji onomastics; Wikipedia, 'Chinese name'

cultures.name: Chinese (Qin, Han & Six Dynasties)
cultures.note: Surname + one-character given name was typical under Han (Wang Mang's era discouraged two-character names); educated men also had a courtesy name (zi). Women often recorded as surname + 'shi' (Wang shi).

sources.cite: China Biographical Database (CBDB), Harvard
Wilkinson, E., Chinese History: A New Manual (2018), ch. on names
de Crespigny, R., A Biographical Dictionary of Later Han to the Three Kingdoms (2007)

cultures.name: Chinese (Sui, Tang & Five Dynasties)
cultures.note: Surname + one- or two-character given name; aristocratic clans (Cui, Lu, Zheng, Wang, Li) dominated. Women often known by birth-order nicknames (Shiliu Niang, '16th lady'). Dunhuang manuscripts give ordinary names.

sources.cite: China Biographical Database (CBDB), Harvard
Wilkinson, E., Chinese History: A New Manual (2018), ch. on names
Dunhuang manuscripts, International Dunhuang Programme

cultures.name: Chinese (Song & Yuan)
cultures.note: Surname + one- or two-character given name; commoners (and many women) were recorded by family number (Sanlang '3rd son', Si Niang '4th daughter') or as surname + shi. Lineages and genealogies grew strongly under Song.

sources.cite: China Biographical Database (CBDB), Harvard
Wilkinson, E., Chinese History: A New Manual (2018), ch. on names
Ebrey, P., The Inner Quarters: Marriage and the Lives of Chinese Women in the Sung Period (1993)

cultures.name: Chinese (Ming & Qing)
cultures.note: Surname + two-character given name, the first character often a generation name (zibei) shared by siblings and cousins from the lineage genealogy. Merchants of Huizhou and Shanxi formed lineage firms. Southern colloquial 'Ah' prefixes for familiar names.

sources.cite: China Biographical Database (CBDB), Harvard
Wilkinson, E., Chinese History: A New Manual (2018), ch. on names
Rowe, W., China's Last Empire: The Great Qing (2009)

cultures.name: Chinese (Republic & PRC)
cultures.note: Surname + one or two characters; mid-century names carry political themes (Jianguo 'build the nation', Weidong 'defend the East'), later shifting to aesthetic two-character names.

sources.cite: China Biographical Database (CBDB), Harvard
Wilkinson, E., Chinese History: A New Manual (2018), ch. on names
Ministry of Public Security name statistics; Wikipedia, 'Chinese given name'

cultures.name: Korean (Three Kingdoms to Joseon & modern)
cultures.note: One-syllable surname (with clan seat bon-gwan, e.g. Gimhae Kim) + usually two-syllable given name with a generation syllable (dollimja). Commoners and slaves of Joseon often lacked surnames until the 1909 registry. 1940s female names in -ja reflect Japanese colonial influence.

sources.cite: Encyclopedia of Korean Culture (AKS)
Wikipedia, 'Korean name'

cultures.name: Japanese (Asuka, Nara & Heian)
cultures.note: Clan name (uji) + 'no' + personal name for aristocrats; women's personal names were rarely recorded, so they are known by court sobriquets (Murasaki Shikibu) or by -ko readings of their names. Commoners lacked surnames.

sources.cite: Plutschow, H., Japan's Name Culture (1995)
Wikipedia, 'Japanese name'
Nihon Kodai Jinmei Jiten (Dictionary of Ancient Japanese Names)

cultures.name: Japanese (Kamakura to Edo)
cultures.note: Samurai had family name + adult name (often numeral -rō or -emon/-bei official-style names); commoners used given names with village/shop names (yagō) and were officially forbidden surnames (myōji) in Edo. Women's names were short, often written in kana with honorific O- (O-Ume).

sources.cite: Plutschow, H., Japan's Name Culture (1995)
Wikipedia, 'Japanese name'
Edo-period shūmon aratamechō (religious registers) studies, e.g. Hayami Akira

cultures.name: Japanese (Meiji to present)
cultures.note: All Japanese took surnames by the 1875 law; family name precedes given name. Women's names in -ko dominated 1900-1980s.

sources.cite: Plutschow, H., Japan's Name Culture (1995)
Wikipedia, 'Japanese name'
Meiji Yasuda Life name ranking (1912-)

cultures.name: Vietnamese (Đại Việt to modern)
cultures.note: Family name + middle name (Văn for men, Thị for women traditionally) + given name; about 40% share the surname Nguyễn. Use pattern '{family} Văn {given}' / '{family} Thị {given}' for commoners.

sources.cite: Wikipedia, 'Vietnamese name'
Taylor, K. W., A History of the Vietnamese (2013)

cultures.name: Khmer (Angkor & post-Angkor)
cultures.note: Angkorian inscriptions record Sanskrit names for elites (-varman, -pandita) and Old Khmer status prefixes for ordinary people (Vap/Ku 'man/woman of humble status', Pon, Ten, Mratan). Modern Khmer: family name + given name, introduced under French rule.

sources.cite: Vickery, M., Society, Economics, and Politics in Pre-Angkor Cambodia (1998)
Corpus des inscriptions khmères, EFEO / CIK database

cultures.name: Tai & Burmese (Sukhothai, Ayutthaya, Bagan, Konbaung)
cultures.note: Neither Thai nor Burmese used surnames premodern; status prefixes mark persons (Thai Nai 'Mr.', Mae/Nang 'Mrs./Miss'; Burmese Maung/U for men, Ma/Daw for women, Nga for commoners). Thai surnames from 1913.

sources.cite: Wikipedia, 'Thai name' and 'Burmese names'
Luce, G. H., Old Burma - Early Pagan (1969)

cultures.name: Javanese, Malay & Indonesian
cultures.note: Javanese traditionally use a single name (often Su- prefix 'good'), changing names at adulthood or marriage; nobility take titles Raden, Mas, Ndoro. Malay names use 'bin/binti' patronymics.

sources.cite: Uhlenbeck, E. M., 'Systematic features of Javanese personal names', Word 25 (1969)
Wikipedia, 'Javanese name'

cultures.name: Philippine (precolonial & Spanish-era Tagalog/Visayan)
cultures.note: Precolonial single names with titles (Datu, Rajah, Lakan); the 1849 Clavería decree assigned Spanish-style surnames from an alphabetical catalog to families town by town.

sources.cite: Catálogo alfabético de apellidos (1849)
Scott, W. H., Barangay: Sixteenth-Century Philippine Culture and Society (1994)

cultures.name: Mongol
cultures.note: Single names, frequently Turkic or later Tibetan-Buddhist (Dorj, Luvsan); people identified by clan (obog) such as Borjigin. Modern Mongolians use father's name as patronym before the given name.

sources.cite: de Rachewiltz, I., The Secret History of the Mongols (2004)
Atwood, C., Encyclopedia of Mongolia and the Mongol Empire (2004)

cultures.name: Old Turkic & Steppe (Göktürk, Uyghur, Khazar, Kipchak)
cultures.note: Names from Orkhon inscriptions and Uyghur documents, often animal/strength words (Arslan 'lion', Böri 'wolf') plus titles (Tegin, Tarkhan, Beg, Khatun) that function as part of the name.

sources.cite: Tekin, T., A Grammar of Orkhon Turkic (1968)
Golden, P., An Introduction to the History of the Turkic Peoples (1992)

cultures.name: Central Asian Turkic-Islamic (Chagatai, Timurid, Uzbek, Kazakh, Uyghur)
cultures.note: Islamic Persian-Arabic given names mixed with Turkic ones; Timurid princes used Mirza, Kazakh lineages tracked by clan (ru) and patronymic -uly/-kyzy; Russian-style -ov/-ova surnames from the 19th-20th c.

sources.cite: Encyclopaedia Iranica / Encyclopaedia of Islam entries on Timurid and Uzbek dynasties
Manz, B. F., Power, Politics and Religion in Timurid Iran (2007)

cultures.name: Tibetan
cultures.note: Two-part given names often bestowed by lamas (Tenzin Gyatso), many unisex; no surnames except aristocratic house names (Doring, Lhalu, Shatra) and day-of-week names (Nyima Sunday, Dawa Monday, Mingma Tuesday, Lhakpa Wednesday, Phurba Thursday, Pasang Friday, Pemba Saturday).

sources.cite: Wikipedia, 'Tibetan name'
Treasury of Lives: biographical encyclopedia of Tibet

cultures.name: Old Norse (Viking Age)
cultures.note: Given name + patronymic (-sson / -dóttir) plus frequent nicknames (Eiríkr inn rauði 'the Red'). Runestones (Sweden especially) attest thousands of ordinary names.

sources.cite: Nordiskt runnamnslexikon (Peterson, L., 2007)
Lind, E. H., Norsk-isländska dopnamn (1905-15)

cultures.name: Anglo-Saxon (Old English)
cultures.note: Single dithematic names (Æthel- 'noble', Wulf- 'wolf', -ric 'ruler'); bynames by place, father ('Godwines sunu') or trade appear in late charters and Domesday.

sources.cite: Prosopography of Anglo-Saxon England (PASE)
Searle, W. G., Onomasticon Anglo-Saxonicum (1897)

cultures.name: Medieval English (Anglo-Norman & Middle English)
cultures.note: Norman given names replaced English ones within a few generations; bynames (locative, occupational, patronymic, nickname) became hereditary surnames 1250-1400.

sources.cite: Reaney, P. H. & Wilson, R. M., A Dictionary of English Surnames (1991)
Withycombe, E. G., Oxford Dictionary of English Christian Names (1977)
Medieval Names Archive, Academy of Saint Gabriel / SCA

cultures.name: Early Modern English (Tudor to Georgian)
cultures.note: Fixed hereditary surnames; Protestant and Puritan given names (biblical, virtue names) rise after 1560. Also used for English colonists in North America.

sources.cite: Smith-Bannister, S., Names and Naming Patterns in England 1538-1700 (1997)
Hanks, P. et al., Oxford Dictionary of Family Names in Britain and Ireland (2016)

cultures.name: Gaelic (Irish & Scottish)
cultures.note: Patronymic 'mac' (son) / 'ingen' (daughter), with clan surnames Ó (grandson/descendant) and Mac fixed from the 10th-12th c.; devotional names 'Máel/Gilla' (servant of).

sources.cite: Ó Corráin, D. & Maguire, F., Irish Names (1990)
Corpus of Electronic Texts (CELT), UCC
Medieval Names Archive, Academy of Saint Gabriel / SCA

cultures.name: Welsh & Brittonic
cultures.note: Patronymic chains (ap/ab 'son of', ferch 'daughter of'); fixed surnames formed from these (ap Hywel > Powell) after the 1536 Acts of Union.

sources.cite: Morgan, T. J. & Morgan, P., Welsh Surnames (1985)
Bartrum, P. C., Welsh Genealogies AD 300-1400 (1974)
Medieval Names Archive, Academy of Saint Gabriel / SCA

cultures.name: Frankish & Early Medieval Germanic (Merovingian, Carolingian, Visigothic, Lombard)
cultures.note: Single dithematic Germanic names (Hildi- 'battle', -berht 'bright', -wulf), recorded in polyptychs (Saint-Germain-des-Prés lists thousands of peasants). Bynames rare before 1000.

sources.cite: Polyptych of Irminon (Saint-Germain-des-Prés), ed. Longnon (1886-95)
Morlet, M.-T., Les noms de personne sur le territoire de l'ancienne Gaule du VIe au XIIe siècle (1968)
Medieval Names Archive, Academy of Saint Gabriel / SCA

cultures.name: Medieval French (Old & Middle French, Occitan)
cultures.note: Given name + byname from place (de X), trade, father, or nickname; hereditary surnames by the 14th c. Tax rolls of Paris (1292, 1313) record thousands of commoners.

sources.cite: Géraud, H., Paris sous Philippe-le-Bel: le rôle de la taille de 1292 (1837)
Dauzat, A., Dictionnaire étymologique des noms de famille et prénoms de France (1951)
Medieval Names Archive, Academy of Saint Gabriel / SCA

cultures.name: Early Modern French (Ancien Régime)
cultures.note: Fixed surnames, given names chosen from godparents and saints; compound names (Jean-Baptiste, Marie-Anne) common after 1650. Also New France and the Antilles.

sources.cite: Dupâquier, J. (ed.), Le prénom: mode et histoire (1984)
Programme de recherche en démographie historique (PRDH), Université de Montréal

cultures.name: Medieval Italian
cultures.note: Given name + patronymic (di X, X's son) or place; Florentine catasto-style names with 'di {father}' were the norm and family names consolidated among elites by 1300.

sources.cite: Herlihy, D. & Klapisch-Zuber, C., Online Catasto of 1427
De Felice, E., Dizionario dei nomi italiani (1986)
Medieval Names Archive, Academy of Saint Gabriel / SCA

cultures.name: Renaissance & Early Modern Italian
cultures.note: Given name + family name, with patronymic 'di' common in records; Venetian dialect forms (Zuan, Alvise). Godparent and saint names dominate after Trent (1563).

sources.cite: Herlihy, D. & Klapisch-Zuber, C., Online Catasto of 1427
De Felice, E., Dizionario dei cognomi italiani (1978)

cultures.name: Castilian / Spanish (medieval & early modern)
cultures.note: Given name + patronymic surname in -ez (Rodrigo Díaz 'son of Diego'), later fixed, often with a toponym (de Vivar). From the 16th c. double surnames; used also in Spanish America (with Nahuatl/Quechua boxes taking precedence where smaller).

sources.cite: Faure, R. et al., Diccionario de apellidos españoles (2001)
Catálogo de Pasajeros a Indias, Archivo General de Indias
Medieval Names Archive, Academy of Saint Gabriel / SCA

cultures.name: Portuguese (medieval & early modern)
cultures.note: As in Castile: patronymics in -es (Fernandes, Gonçalves) plus toponyms; Portuguese naming spread to Brazil, Goa, Atlantic islands and African coasts.

sources.cite: Machado, J. P., Dicionário Onomástico Etimológico da Língua Portuguesa (1984)
Arquivo Nacional Torre do Tombo

cultures.name: Medieval German
cultures.note: Germanic dithematic names give way to saints' names after 1200; surnames from trades (Müller, Schmid), places (von X) and fathers become hereditary in towns 1250-1450.

sources.cite: Bahlow, H., Deutsches Namenlexikon (1967)
Socin, A., Mittelhochdeutsches Namenbuch nach oberrheinischen Quellen (1903)
Medieval Names Archive, Academy of Saint Gabriel / SCA

cultures.name: Early Modern German
cultures.note: Fixed surnames; Rufname often the second of two baptismal names (Johann Georg called Georg). Lutheran and Catholic regions differ (Catholic Maria, Joseph, Ignaz).

sources.cite: Kohlheim, R. & V., Duden Familiennamen (2005)
Deutsches Familiennamenwörterbuch (DFD)

cultures.name: Dutch & Flemish (Golden Age)
cultures.note: Patronymics (Jansz = Jan's son, Pietersdr) were standard for most people; fixed surnames (often 'van' + place) spread among burghers; universal surnames enforced only in 1811. Also New Netherland, the Cape and Batavia.

sources.cite: Meertens Instituut, Nederlandse Voornamenbank & Familienamenbank
Ebeling, R. A., Voornamen in Nederland (1993)

cultures.name: West Slavic (Polish, Czech, Slovak)
cultures.note: Old Slavic dithematic names (-sław 'glory', -mir 'peace') and Christian names; noble surnames in -ski/-cki (from estates) from the 15th c., peasants by patronymic or nickname until the 18th c.

sources.cite: Taszycki, W. et al., Słownik staropolskich nazw osobowych (1965-87)
Svoboda, J., Staročeská osobní jména a naše příjmení (1964)

cultures.name: East Slavic (Kievan Rus' to Imperial Russia, Ruthenian)
cultures.note: Pre-Christian Slavic names gave way to Orthodox calendar names; patronymics (-ovich/-ich, -ovna) universal, with family names among nobility from the 15th c. and common people by the 18th-19th c. Birchbark letters of Novgorod attest commoners.

sources.cite: Tupikov, N. M., Slovar' drevnerusskikh lichnykh sobstvennykh imen (1903)
Gramoty.ru: Novgorod birchbark letters corpus

cultures.name: Hungarian (Magyar)
cultures.note: Hungarian places family name before given name. Pagan Magyar names (Árpád, Emese) gave way to Christian ones; surnames from places (-i: Szegedi), trades and nicknames by the 15th c.

sources.cite: Fehértói, K., Árpád-kori személynévtár (1004-1356) (2004)
Kázmér, M., Régi magyar családnevek szótára (1993)

cultures.name: South Slavic (Serbian, Bulgarian, Croatian, Bosnian)
cultures.note: Slavic names with Orthodox/Catholic saints' names; patronymic surnames in -ić/-ović (Serbo-Croatian) and -ov/-ev (Bulgarian) fixed in the 18th-19th c.

sources.cite: Grković, M., Rečnik ličnih imena kod Srba (1977)
Ilchev, S., Rechnik na lichnite i familnite imena u balgarite (1969)

cultures.name: Baltic & Finnic (Lithuanian, Latvian, Finnish, Estonian)
cultures.note: Lithuanian dithematic pagan names among nobility, Christian names after 1387; Latvian and Estonian peasants received surnames only in the 1820s-30s; Finns used farm names and patronymics.

sources.cite: Zinkevičius, Z., Lietuvių asmenvardžiai (2008)
Finnish Names Archive, Institute for the Languages of Finland

cultures.name: Nahua (Aztec / colonial Nahuatl)
cultures.note: Calendrical day names (Ce Acatl 'One Reed') and descriptive names; birth-order names for women (Tiacapan 'first-born', Tlaco 'middle', Xocoyotl 'youngest'). After 1521 a Spanish baptismal name preceded the Nahuatl name.

sources.cite: Lockhart, J., The Nahuas After the Conquest (1992)
Online Nahuatl Dictionary (Wired Humanities Projects), personal names

cultures.name: Maya (Classic & Postclassic / colonial Yucatec)
cultures.note: Classic royal names combine deity and animal elements (K'inich 'sun-faced', Bahlam 'jaguar'); Yucatec Maya had patrilineal surnames (chibal: Chi, Pech, Couoh, Xiu) with Ah/Ix (male/female) prefixes; colonial Maya kept them after Christian names.

sources.cite: Martin, S. & Grube, N., Chronicle of the Maya Kings and Queens (2008)
Restall, M., The Maya World: Yucatec Culture and Society 1550-1850 (1997)

cultures.name: Andean (Inca Quechua & Aymara, colonial)
male: Juan de Santa Cruz Pachacuti Yamqui
cultures.note: Single Quechua names (Quispe 'free', Sisa 'flower', Ocllo 'pure') with lineage (panaca, ayllu) membership; after the conquest a Spanish Christian name plus the Quechua or Aymara name became a hereditary surname.

sources.cite: Guaman Poma de Ayala, El primer nueva corónica y buen gobierno (1615), Royal Danish Library
Rostworowski, M., History of the Inca Realm (1999)

cultures.name: Eastern Woodlands (Algonquian & Iroquoian)
cultures.note: Names were personal, changed across life stages and achievements, and are known mostly from colonial records in English/French spellings. Iroquoian chiefly titles (Hiawatha, Deganawida) pass within clans. Lists are short and selective.

sources.cite: Goddard, I. & Bragdon, K., Native Writings in Massachusett (1988)
Handbook of North American Indians, Vol. 15: Northeast (Smithsonian, 1978)

cultures.name: Hawaiian
cultures.note: Single names, often long and commemorating events or ancestors, with aliʻi (chiefly) genealogies; after 1860 a Christian first name plus Hawaiian name, made a surname by the Act of 1860.

sources.cite: Pukui, M. K. & Elbert, S. H., Hawaiian Dictionary (1986), name glossary
Kamakau, S. M., Ruling Chiefs of Hawaii (1961)

cultures.name: Māori & other Polynesian (Tahitian, Tongan, Samoan)
cultures.note: Single names drawn from ancestors and events, tied to whakapapa (genealogy) and iwi/hapū identity; Christian transliterated names (Wiremu = William) after missionary contact; later used as surnames.

sources.cite: Te Ara: The Encyclopedia of New Zealand
Dictionary of New Zealand Biography

cultures.name: Aboriginal Australian (colonial-era records)
cultures.note: Hundreds of language groups with their own naming and kin systems; names here are those recorded (often imperfectly) in colonial documents for Sydney, Victoria, Tasmania and Western Australia. Thin, selective list.

sources.cite: Australian Dictionary of Biography
AIATSIS

cultures.name: Modern English (UK, US, Canada, Australia, NZ)
cultures.note: Fixed surnames with one or two given names; 19th-c. names highly concentrated (John, William, Mary), diversifying through the 20th c. Covers British settler societies.

sources.cite: UK Office for National Statistics, Baby Names in England and Wales
US Social Security Administration, Popular Baby Names (from 1880)

cultures.name: Modern French
cultures.note: Fixed surnames; given names limited by the 1803 law to calendar saints and historical figures until 1966. Also Belgium, Québec and French North Africa (settlers).

sources.cite: INSEE, Fichier des prénoms (from 1900)
Geneanet surname statistics

cultures.name: Modern German (Germany, Austria, Switzerland)
cultures.note: Fixed surnames, many occupational; given names in multiple forms (Johann Friedrich) through the 19th c. Popularity shifts rapidly in the 20th c.

sources.cite: Kohlheim, R. & V., Duden Familiennamen (2005)
Bielefeld, K., beliebte-vornamen.de historical rankings

cultures.name: Modern Italian
cultures.note: Fixed surnames with strong regional distributions (Esposito in Naples, Brambilla in Lombardy); given names often from grandparents.

sources.cite: ISTAT, Nomi dei nati
De Felice, E., Dizionario dei cognomi italiani (1978)

cultures.name: Modern Spanish & Latin American
cultures.note: Two surnames: father's first surname then mother's first surname (Juan García López). Compound Marian names (María de los Dolores) common.

sources.cite: INE Spain, Apellidos y nombres más frecuentes
Faure, R. et al., Diccionario de apellidos españoles (2001)

cultures.name: Modern Portuguese & Brazilian
cultures.note: Mother's surname then father's surname (the last is the main one), often with 'de/da/dos'. Brazilian naming is more inventive (Washington, Wellington) from the 1940s.

sources.cite: IBGE Nomes no Brasil (Censo 2010)
Instituto dos Registos e do Notariado, Portugal

cultures.name: Modern Russian (Imperial & Soviet)
cultures.note: Given name + patronymic + surname; women's patronymics -ovna/-evna and surnames -ova/-eva. Soviet-era neologisms (Vilen, Marlen) appear 1920s-30s.

sources.cite: Superanskaya, A. V., Slovar' russkikh lichnykh imen (1998)
Unbegaun, B., Russian Surnames (1972)

cultures.name: Modern Indian (British Raj & Republic)
cultures.note: Hindu surnames from caste/community (Sharma, Patel, Iyer) or village/father's name, especially in the south where initials often replace surnames; Muslims, Sikhs (Singh/Kaur) and Parsis have their own conventions.

sources.cite: Census of India
Wikipedia, 'Indian name'

cultures.name: Modern Persian (Iran, Afghanistan, Tajikistan)
cultures.note: Surnames mandated in 1925 (Iran), often from place (Tehrani), trade, title, or chosen words (-i, -zadeh 'born of', -pour 'son of').

sources.cite: Statistical Centre of Iran / Civil Registration Organization
Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Family Names'
